warnings: Take at the start of the headache, not during the aura: a dose taken during the aura is ineffective.
Triptan use on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more days, risks medication-overuse headache; caffeine-containing combination analgesics count toward the 10-day limit.
High daily caffeine intake is associated with more frequent headache, and abrupt withdrawal causes withdrawal headache; reduce gradually.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Make the diagnosis of migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) on clinical grounds: no red flag is present, so no neuroimaging is needed.
Start sumatriptan 50-100 mg at headache onset (not during the aura), which may be combined with ibuprofen 400-600 mg, with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg) for nausea.
Address triggers: regular sleep, stress management, and a gradual reduction of caffeine (about one cup less each week) to avoid withdrawal headache.

Keep a headache diary; if disabling headache days stay at 2 or more a month after the trigger changes, discuss preventive treatment (AHS 2021), choosing an agent compatible with her contraception and pregnancy plans.
Advise that combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring) is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; if contraception is wanted, offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in the MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM trials.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; it has a role only when cardioembolic stroke is in question.

differential.key_features: A reproducible, stereotyped visual aura precedes every headache: this is migraine with aura.
Aura spreading over 20-25 min is too slow for seizure propagation; no impaired awareness
No papilloedema, episodic rather than daily headache, normal BMI (21.3), normal examination.
Severe unilateral throbbing with photophobia, phonophobia and nausea is migrainous, not tension-type

key_clinical_evidence: Classic visual aura (expanding scintillating scotoma) over 20-25 min followed by headache is the most common form of migraine aura
Routine MRI is not indicated when ICHD-3 criteria are met and the examination is normal [AHS_neuroimaging_2020]
Increasing frequency with identifiable triggers (stress, sleep, caffeine) is a treatment question, not a reason for diagnostic testing
Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The attacks began at 19, years before the PhD, and are stereotyped; high caffeine intake raises attack frequency but does not change the diagnosis; address it as a modifiable trigger
red_herrings.data_point: High caffeine intake (3-4 cups a day) as a possible cause of secondary headache
red_herrings.intended_effect: High caffeine intake can cause daily or medication-overuse headache and may distract from the migraine diagnosis

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks since age 19: 8-10 a year, rising to about 2 a month over the past 6 months.
Visual only: paracentral scotoma expanding into a shimmering crescent that moves into one hemifield (either side). No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Gradual expansion over 20-25 min; fully reversible.
Unilateral throbbing headache, usually right-sided, 7/10, after the aura resolves, with nausea and photophobia; lasts 4-8 h. About 2 headache days a month now, with missed study days.
Stress, irregular sleep, 3-4 cups of coffee a day. Ibuprofen 400-600 mg partly effective; triptan-naive.
Headache-free. Normal cranial nerves, visual fields by confrontation, no papilloedema; normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. BP 110/68 mmHg.

Systemic symptoms or fever: absent. Neoplasia history: absent. Neurological deficit between attacks: absent. Sudden onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 19). Pattern change: frequency increase with identifiable triggers, aura and headache character unchanged. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: not reported. Aura always on the same side: absent. No red flag present.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent fully reversible visual aura with gradual spread over 20-25 min, followed by headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.1.1 typical aura with headache (criterion C 5 of 6). Frequency rising with stress, sleep disruption and high caffeine intake. No red flag; normal examination.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 24-year-old Chinese-American woman presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of recurrent headaches with visual phenomena that started at age 19. Until recently she had approximately 8-10 attacks per year. Each begins with a small blind spot near the center of her vision that gradually expands over 20-25 minutes into a bright, shimmering, crescent-shaped arc that sweeps into the periphery of one side of her vision (either side) and then disappears. Following the resolution of the visual phenomenon, she develops a moderate-to-severe unilateral throbbing headache (typically right-sided, 7/10 intensity) with nausea and sensitivity to light, lasting 4-8 hours. She has missed several days of university and now graduate school due to these headaches.

She notes an increase in attack frequency to about two a month since starting her PhD program 6 months ago, attributing it to stress, irregular sleep, and frequent caffeine intake (3-4 cups coffee daily). Her mother and maternal grandmother both had migraines throughout their reproductive years. She takes over-the-counter ibuprofen which gives partial relief. She has not tried triptans. She is not on oral contraceptives. She had a normal physical examination with her university health provider 4 months ago. She denies any limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, or any episodes that differ from her typical pattern.
